_note: Quiz and true-or-false items written but not yet blind-checked; apply_check.py moves checked items onto the site.

item.statement: Fewer people call themselves atheists after a DMT 'being' encounter, and after drug-free 'God' encounters too.
item.why: Among people who'd had such meetings, 28 in 100 recalled being atheists before a DMT encounter and 10 in 100 said they were now, and the share fell without drugs too. But they were recalling old beliefs years later.

item.statement: Most volunteers in one lab study ranked a single psilocybin session among their 5 most meaningful experiences.
item.why: Two months later, 67 in 100 did. But everyone in that study already took part in religious or spiritual activities, which may have made them see it as more spiritual.

item.statement: A meth overdose shows up as slow breathing and tiny pupils.
item.why: It's the reverse: it looks like a body in overdrive, with a racing heart, fast breathing, wide pupils and great restlessness. That's second-hand, from two reviews of hospital studies, and how often each sign shows up varies a lot.

item.statement: The more traditional the ayahuasca ceremony, the less fear people feel.
item.why: In one big survey, more traditional practices went with a little more fear, and church hymns or sermons with less. The differences were small, and people rated everything looking back.

item.statement: Lots of people who take magic mushrooms end up seeking emergency treatment.
item.why: In one big online survey, about 2 in 1,000 people who'd used them in the past year said they had, and nearly all of those felt back to normal within a day. But nobody checked their answers, and anyone who couldn't answer wasn't counted.

item.statement: Other people's cannabis smoke can never make you fail a urine drug test.
item.why: After an hour in a sealed, smoky room, 1 of 18 people who didn't smoke went over the US government's workplace limit, and 12 tested positive at least once at a lower limit some private tests use. That was one small lab test, mostly in thick smoke, not everyday smoke.

item.statement: In lab tests, fentanyl test strips often missed fentanyl that was really there.
item.why: Strips showed fentanyl in 104 of 106 police-seized samples that had it. But trained lab staff did the tests, mostly with one brand, and testing at home wasn't studied.

item.statement: One ketamine drip can lift depression within hours.
item.why: A day after one drip, 64 in 100 were much better, against 28 in 100 after a sedative drip. But for most the lift faded within weeks, and people can often tell they got ketamine, which may make it look bigger.

item.statement: In a big trial for hard-to-treat depression, psilocybin's benefit was still clear after 12 weeks.
item.why: By 12 weeks, the gap with the comparison group could be chance. People could probably tell they'd taken psilocybin, and nobody checked, which may have made the earlier gap look bigger.

item.statement: Teens who remembered more of the US government's anti-drug ads were, if anything, more likely to try cannabis.
item.why: In a national survey, they were no less likely to start, fewer said they definitely wouldn't, and in one of three periods more ads went with more first use. The authors call that tentative, not definitive.

item.statement: In older US surveys, about 9 in 100 people who ever tried cannabis became dependent.
item.why: In the first survey, that was fewer than for tobacco, heroin, cocaine or alcohol. The surveys ran from 1990 to 2005 and used a narrower definition; newer US figures that count milder cases are higher.

item.statement: Almost everyone who tries stimulants like meth gets hooked.
item.why: It depends how you count: an old US survey found about 11 in 100 had ever been dependent, and a broader Australian count estimated about 50 in 100 within 14 years. Neither had a number for meth alone.

item.statement: In UK reports, most people with low blood salt after MDMA had drunk a lot of liquid.
item.why: At least 10 of 17 cases reported to a UK poisons service had, and the 2 who died had brain swelling. These reports count only people who got ill, so they can't show how often it happens or whether drinking more changes the risk.

item.statement: If a friend took the same MDMA and didn't overheat, you won't either.
item.why: Nobody can yet say why some people get hotter than others: in one case of severe overheating, a friend who took the same MDMA didn't overheat. That's second-hand, from one review of small studies and cases.

item.statement: Most men who used cannabis heavily never went to hospital with schizophrenia, in a big Swedish study.
item.why: About 38 in 1,000 men who'd used it more than 50 times later did, against about 6 in 1,000 who had never used it. These counts don't allow for other differences between the men.

item.statement: Weed really is stronger than it used to be, on average.
item.why: Across 7 countries from 1970 to 2017, THC, its main active part, rose about 3 points every 10 years in weed and 6 in hash. But most samples were seized by police, so they may not match what people buy.

item.statement: Teen cannabis use has been shown to lower IQ later in life.
item.why: In one New Zealand study, people dependent on it for years lost about 6 points from their childhood scores. Another researcher showed family background could produce a similar pattern; the first team found it didn't change their result.

item.statement: On average, people who often use cannabis score a little lower on memory tests.
item.why: A big review found small gaps in learning, memory, attention and planning, but none clear for language, shape or movement. People were tested only after they'd started, so it can't show cannabis caused the gap.

item.statement: The 2002 study claiming ecstasy harmed monkeys' brains had actually given the animals a different drug.
item.why: The drug came from a wrongly labelled bottle, and the study was withdrawn a year later. The withdrawal notice doesn't say what the one animal that got ecstasy showed.

item.statement: All antidepressants carry about the same serotonin risk when mixed with ecstasy.
item.why: One 2007 review ranked MAOI antidepressants highest and SSRI-type antidepressants lower. That's the authors' judgment from reports and how the drugs work; no study counted how often each mix causes harm.

item.statement: Worldwide, alcohol is estimated to cause millions of deaths a year.
item.why: Global models put it at about 2.3 to 2.8 million a year, against a world where no one drank, and at ages 15 to 49 it was the top risk factor in one study. These are computer estimates, not counted deaths.

item.statement: In a UK expert ranking of 20 drugs, tobacco scored zero for deaths like overdose.
item.why: Lung cancer was counted elsewhere, and the authors agreed tobacco probably kills more than the other 19 drugs combined. The scores are one panel's views, not measures.

item.statement: People who had taken more ecstasy showed less of a serotonin marker, in most studies.
item.why: Four studies found this link and two smaller ones didn't. But amounts came from memory, and people who take more ecstasy also take more of other drugs.

item.statement: In lab tests, men told their drink had vodka drank more, whatever was really in it.
item.why: They drank about twice as much in 15 minutes, while real vodka made no clear difference to how much they drank. These were lab tests from the 1970s and 1980s, with low blood alcohol.

item.statement: When meth's good feelings fade over days of use, the bad effects fade too.
item.why: In a small lab study, the good feelings were gone within three days, while dizziness, sickness and a pounding heart grew and appetite stayed down. Only six to nine people took part, on small doses.

item.statement: More people finish opioid withdrawal treatment on buprenorphine than on clonidine or lofexidine.
item.why: In 14 trials, about 72 in 100 finished on buprenorphine, against about 45 on the other medicines, and withdrawal was milder on average. No trial reported people coming off fentanyl.

item.statement: If an antidepressant mutes MDMA's effects, that means less MDMA is in your blood.
item.why: In small trials, two antidepressants lowered how strongly people rated MDMA's effects, yet the MDMA peak in their blood was about 15 to 18 percent higher. That's second-hand, from single trials of 16 healthy people each.

item.statement: In safety reports about ecstasy, cases that also named an antidepressant more often ended in death.
item.why: In US reports, those cases had about 1.6 times the odds of a fatal outcome, and reports naming muscle relaxants or anesthetics had higher odds still. These are voluntary reports, so they can't show cause, and nobody knows how many people took each mix.

item.statement: Children adopted away from a birth parent with a drug problem still have drug problems more often.
item.why: In a Swedish study, about 9 in 100 of them had one on record, against 4 in 100 when neither birth parent did. What birth parents pass on includes the pregnancy, not just genes.

item.statement: People who took GHB or GBL with alcohol more often ended up in critical care than those without.
item.why: Of emergency patients kept in hospital, 55 in 100 who'd also had alcohol went to critical care, against 22 in 100 without. Alcohol use was reported, not measured, and the amounts weren't known.

item.statement: In most published 'excited delirium' deaths, force such as restraint was recorded.
item.why: Force, including sedation and electrical weapons as well as restraint, was recorded in 94 of 104 deaths among published cases. These were selected reports, so they can't tell how much restraint, drugs or the agitated state caused a death.

item.statement: Colour test kits for MDMA are easy to read, even for first-timers.
item.why: In one small 2003 lab study, two people new to the kit made many mistakes: one missed both MDMA samples, and the other called four other drugs MDMA. Lab experts got MDMA right.

item.statement: In one study, people off heavy cannabis use for a year or more scored like people who hadn't used.
item.why: They scored no differently on any test, and a big review found smaller gaps in studies that asked people to stop for over 3 days. But few studies have followed people that long, and researchers disagree.

item.statement: People who microdose can't tell a real microdose from a dummy capsule.
item.why: In trials, people guessed right about 7 times in 10, and their ratings followed what they believed they'd taken. Feeling an effect may have shaped that belief.

item.statement: Police officers have had confirmed overdoses from just touching fentanyl.
item.why: None has been confirmed: a federal safety agency looked into cases where officers felt ill and found no signs of a serious overdose, though no officer had a test that finds fentanyl. Finding no proven case isn't proof it never happens.

item.statement: One dose of meth leaves people sadder and craving it the next morning.
item.why: In one small lab study, the biggest dose left people less alert and friendly the next morning than a dummy dose, but not sadder or more worried, and they didn't want meth more. Only eleven people took part, in a hospital unit.

item.statement: In one US survey, about 14 in 100 adults had alcohol use disorder in the past year.
item.why: Two or more of 11 signs of problem drinking in a year count, and about half the cases were mild. Another US survey found a little over half as many, so the number depends on the survey.

item.statement: Studies show people who drink a little live longer than people who never drank.
item.why: Many studies found slightly fewer deaths in people who drink a little, but compared with people who had never drunk, there was no clear difference. Few studies made that comparison, so a small gain or a small loss is still possible.

item.statement: In gene studies, drinking more went with more strokes, especially bleeding in the brain.
item.why: In a big study of Chinese adults, men whose genes made them drink more had more strokes, and bleeding strokes rose most. Women, who mostly don't drink, showed no link with the same genes.

item.statement: Early dementia can itself lead to benzodiazepine prescriptions.
item.why: Worry and poor sleep can come before dementia and lead to these prescriptions, and neither of two big studies could rule that out. In one, the authors said early symptoms may explain a small extra risk with light or moderate use.

item.statement: Caffeine doesn't really change how much you sleep that night.
item.why: Across 24 studies comparing nights with and without caffeine in the same people, they slept about 45 minutes less after caffeine, and their sleep was lighter. These were healthy adults with low to moderate usual intake, so heavy users, teenagers and older adults may differ.

item.statement: In small trials, cannabis medicines controlled sickness from chemotherapy better than a dummy did.
item.why: About 47 in 100 on a cannabis medicine had their sickness fully controlled, against 20 in 100 on a dummy. But only 102 people were in these three trials, and most trials in the review had serious weaknesses.

item.statement: When deaths were blamed on mephedrone, tests always found the drug in the body.
item.why: By October 2011, 128 deaths in the UK and nearby islands had been linked to it, and tests after death found none in 25. A negative test may miss earlier use, and a positive one doesn't prove cause.

item.statement: Levamisole, an animal worm medicine often found in cocaine around 2010, has been linked to blood and skin harm.
item.why: Case reports describe infection-fighting white blood cells falling very low, and painful purple skin patches, sometimes with dying skin. But since most cocaine held it, finding it shows exposure, not that it caused the harm, and how often harm happens is unknown.

item.statement: Making fentanyl test strips legal has been shown to cut drug deaths.
item.why: After the laws, deaths ran about 7 in 100 below the expected trend, but the study didn't check whether more people used strips, and the drop came in each law's very first month. Other changes at the same time could explain it.

item.statement: There's one agreed way to count a death as a drug death.
item.why: Lists use different rules, some counting drug poisoning as the main cause and others drugs found in tests. In Norway, only about 49 in 100 deaths were on both of two lists, and in Sweden fewer than half.

item.statement: Passing out from GHB again and again has been linked to worse memory.
item.why: In one Dutch study, people who had passed out many times remembered worse than people who used GHB regularly without passing out, and than people who used other drugs. It can't show GHB caused it, and nobody checked whether memory improves.

item.statement: People whose depression lifted on esketamine relapsed more often when switched to a dummy spray.
item.why: Of those switched to a dummy spray, 45 in 100 relapsed, against 27 in 100 who kept esketamine. The company behind it paid for the trials, and critics argue some relapses may be effects of stopping, which the trial couldn't tell apart.

item.statement: Ketamine drips for depression cause memory loss as often as ECT does.
item.why: In a Swedish trial, 19 of 90 had memory loss lasting over a day after ECT, against none of 91 after ketamine drips. Everyone knew which treatment they got.

item.statement: People who use ecstasy score worse on memory tests even if they use hardly any other drug.
item.why: In one study where breath, urine and hair tests checked that people used little else, memory scores didn't differ from others in the same all-night dance scene. Medium-sized differences couldn't be ruled out, and heavier use went with worse scores on one planning test.

item.statement: Bupropion and modafinil have been shown to help people stop using meth.
item.why: Across five trials, about 1 in 5 had stopped by the end, whether on medicine or a dummy pill. The trials were small, so a modest benefit or harm can't be ruled out.

item.statement: Brain scans prove that meth kills dopamine nerve cells.
item.why: Scans show less of one dopamine protein in people who used heavily, but it can drop without nerve cells dying, and other markers aren't always lower. Experts disagree, and nobody has shown it either way.

item.statement: Parkinson's disease is common in people diagnosed with meth or amphetamine problems.
item.why: In Utah health records of people with such diagnoses and no other drug or alcohol diagnosis, it was diagnosed about 3 times as often, but that's about 3 in 1,000 over about 7 years, against 1 in 1,000. Some diagnoses were probably other movement conditions.

item.statement: In most recent US overdose deaths involving meth, meth was the only drug.
item.why: Medical examiners' reports from 2021 to mid-2024 found fentanyl or other opioids in about 7 in 10 of these deaths. That's a different kind of record from the yearly death counts.

item.statement: The link between cannabis and car crashes stays just as strong when studies allow for drinking.
item.why: It shrinks: studies that allowed for alcohol found about 1.1 to 1.2 times the odds of a crash, against 1.7 to 1.8 in studies that didn't. These compare crashed drivers with others, so they can't show one driver's chance of crashing.

item.statement: In doctors' reports of harm from laughing gas, numbness or tingling was the most common problem.
item.why: Of 100 people in published reports, 80 had numbness or tingling and 58 had trouble walking. Not all used it for fun: 25 had been given it in surgery.

item.statement: A study found ketamine trips feel like near-death experiences.
item.why: Only words were compared: a computer checked the words in about 15,000 online trip reports against 625 near-death accounts. Nobody showed the experiences themselves feel alike.

item.statement: MDMA therapy papers left out side effects that their own trial records listed.
item.why: More than half of the less serious problems in the trial records never made it into the papers, and neither did 4 of 13 serious ones, all 4 in people on MDMA. Most studies also noted only problems people raised themselves.

item.statement: People on methadone become fully tolerant to its effect on breathing.
item.why: In two studies of people on methadone, tolerance to its effect on breathing was not complete. Reviews add that tolerance may drop during a break from opioids, so the usual amount may hit much harder, breathing included.

item.statement: Music has been shown to make ketamine treatment for depression work better.
item.why: Nobody knows yet whether it changes how well ketamine works. In a trial of 32 patients, the top blood pressure number rose about 7 points less with music, and the report gave no results on how sessions felt.

item.statement: Bad trips are fairly common among people who've used psychedelics.
item.why: 41 in 100 people who'd used psychedelics recalled at least one difficult trip, and 5 in 100 said one had badly affected their daily life. That's one online survey of US adults looking back over their whole lives.

item.statement: Portugal's drug arrests fell mostly because having drugs for your own use stopped being a crime.
item.why: It became an offence handled by regional panels instead, so those cases left the crime count: crime arrests for drugs fell from over 14,000 to between 5,000 and 5,500 a year.

item.statement: With opioids, take-home fentanyl strips showed fentanyl about as often as tests by trained staff.
item.why: In British Columbia, 90 in 100 take-home results on opioids showed fentanyl, against 89 in 100 on site; with meth and cocaine, home strips showed it far more often. The two groups tested different samples, and no lab checked which results were right.

item.statement: In MDMA trials for PTSD, many people given a dummy pill plus therapy also no longer had PTSD.
item.why: 27 to 39 in 100 on the dummy pill no longer had PTSD about 4 months later, against 61 to 70 in 100 on MDMA. In the trial that asked, most knew which pill they'd had, so expectations may explain part of the gap.

item.statement: Psilocybin has been shown to help people quit smoking.
item.why: In one small study, 12 of just 15 people given psilocybin plus lots of counselling weren't smoking 6 months later. With no comparison group, no one can tell what psilocybin added.

item.statement: The review that found DARE made no difference only tested the original classes, not the 2001 rebuild.
item.why: All 11 studies in the 2004 review, covering over 11,000 students, looked at the original classes; the version rebuilt in 2001 wasn't part of it. So it says nothing either way about the newer classes.

item.statement: Most people who start using cocaine are hooked within a year.
item.why: In US surveys, about 5 in 100 people who had used only powder were dependent within a year of starting, and about 22 in 100 of those who went on to crack. People answered once, so the surveys can't show crack itself made the difference.

item.statement: A US survey found tobacco hooked a bigger share of people who'd used it than cocaine or meth-like stimulants.
item.why: Tobacco 32 in 100, cocaine 17, stimulants other than cocaine about 11, in an early-1990s survey that included people who'd only just started. A broader Australian count, done differently, estimated about 50 in 100 for stimulants within 14 years of starting.

item.statement: Among people who got ill after MDMA, low blood salt was more common in women than men.
item.why: In one poison-centre study, 52 in 100 women tested had low blood salt, against 22 in 100 men. It counted only people ill enough to be reported and tested, so it can't say who's most at risk among everyone who takes MDMA.

item.statement: Cannabis medicines work much better than a dummy medicine for long-lasting pain.
item.why: In combined trials, pain was only about half a point lower out of 10 than with a dummy medicine. The trials were short, mostly tested one mouth spray, and many had weaknesses.

item.statement: Teens who use the most cannabis are a bit more likely to be depressed as young adults.
item.why: Across seven long-term studies, teens in the highest-use group had about 1.4 times the odds of depression as young adults. That's a link, not proof: other differences between the teens may explain it.

item.statement: In one study, daily use of strong cannabis went with about 5 times the odds of psychosis.
item.why: That's compared with never using, in 11 places in Europe and Brazil. Daily use of weaker types went with about 2 times, and the gap between strong and weaker could be chance.

item.statement: Teens who use the most cannabis report suicidal thoughts and attempts more often than teens who don't.
item.why: A review of three studies each found about 1.5 times the odds of suicidal thoughts and 3.5 times the odds of attempts in teens who used the most. That can't show cause: in other studies, the link shrank or went away once depression, alcohol and hard living conditions were counted.

item.statement: Stopping regular cannabis use can mess with your sleep and bring strange dreams.
item.why: Between about a third and three quarters of people with withdrawal symptoms had sleep problems, often with strange dreams for days or weeks, and in the lab they took longer to fall asleep. That's second-hand, from a review that didn't check how good the studies were.

item.statement: Memory bounces back once people stop using ecstasy, research shows.
item.why: Nobody knows yet: in a few small studies, people who had stopped for at least 6 months scored about the same as people still using, and both scored lower than people who had never used. But these compared different people, not the same people over time.

item.statement: Brain scans prove that ecstasy destroys serotonin nerve cells.
item.why: Four teams found less of a serotonin marker in the outer brain of people who use ecstasy, but less marker can also mean cells make less of it, not that cells are gone. Nobody was scanned before they started, and these groups also used more other drugs.

item.statement: Muscle jerks and shaking are key signs doctors look for in serotonin syndrome.
item.why: Doctors check for muscle jerks, shaking with very brisk reflexes, sweating and restlessness, and in severe cases stiff muscles with a high fever. A checklist of these signs was tested in one hospital unit, on overdoses.

item.statement: The day after some benzo sleeping pills, people drove worse than with alcohol at a common drink-driving limit.
item.why: In tests in a real car or a driving machine, weaving inside the lane was worse with some pills than with alcohol at the limit used in several countries. Most studies tested one night in healthy volunteers, not people who take these pills for months.

item.statement: Caffeine makes people who rarely have it more alert.
item.why: In one lab study, caffeine made them faster but raised their jitters, not their alertness. It's one study, and people chose their own caffeine habits.

item.statement: A psychedelic flashback means reliving the whole trip for hours.
item.why: In Swiss lab studies of LSD and psilocybin, a flashback was usually a few seconds of changed seeing, mostly in the days after, and most people didn't mind it. These were healthy, screened volunteers, with no drug-free group to compare.

item.statement: People with no working version of the enzyme that clears MDMA get far higher levels of it.
item.why: Their peak level was only about 15 percent higher, and only in the first 3 hours: MDMA seems to switch that enzyme off itself, so these body differences matter less. Just 7 such people were studied.

item.statement: Only a few psychiatric medicines have been tested together with MDMA in studies.
item.why: Each was tested once, in 14 to 16 healthy people, and results differed: with MDMA, the antipsychotic haloperidol lowered well-being and raised anxiety. For several others, a 2022 review found no controlled study at all.

item.statement: Rat Park has been repeated, with the same result.
item.why: Two later experiments meant to repeat the 1981 Rat Park morphine study did not find the same result. In the original studies, the two groups also drank from different machines, measured differently, and all of it was in rats.

item.statement: Alcohol is listed in about 1 in 7 US opioid overdose deaths.
item.why: Death certificates have listed alcohol in about 15 of 100 opioid overdose deaths, a share steady since 2008, and more often for men than women. Alcohol is often left off death records, and counts like these can't say how much it adds to risk.

item.statement: The LSD chromosome scare began with LSD added to blood cells in a lab dish.
item.why: The cells came from just two people, plus one patient who had no 'before' test. The studies that followed, up to 1970, also looked only at blood cells under a microscope, not at sperm or eggs.

item.statement: When testing at one festival showed a drug wasn't as sold, most people handed drugs over to be destroyed.
item.why: At an English festival, 30 of 45 people whose drug wasn't as sold handed drugs over, against 15 of 164 whose drug matched. That was one festival with chemists doing the testing, and people may have kept other drugs.

item.statement: Pills like Adderall give healthy people a big boost on thinking tests.
item.why: Across 48 studies of a single pill of amphetamine or methylphenidate, the average lift was small, clearest for holding back an automatic response. Daily use, studying and exams weren't tested.

item.statement: Benzos were listed in about 1 in 5 US opioid overdose deaths in 2017.
item.why: That's 21 in 100 death certificates, up from 9 in 1999, with benzos listed more often alongside prescription opioids or methadone than heroin or fentanyl. Records miss some drugs, and a share of deaths doesn't measure risk.

item.statement: Bladder problems linked to ketamine never ease, even after people stop using it.
item.why: In one survey, 128 of 251 people who described how their symptoms changed said they eased after stopping. No study has compared people who stopped with people who kept using, though.

item.statement: Drinking alcohol was estimated to cause about 4 in 100 new cancers worldwide in 2020.
item.why: A model put it at 741,000 new cancers, about 6 in 100 in men and 2 in 100 in women, led by gullet, liver, breast and bowel cancer. It's a computer estimate built on risks from studies of groups, not a count.

item.statement: In a UK scan study, 35 in 100 people who barely drank had a memory area rated 'shrunken'.
item.why: 'Shrunken' meant doctors saw any sign of shrinkage at all. People who drank more got the rating more often, but the study can't show alcohol caused it.

item.statement: Most people treated in hospital for alcohol withdrawal get the DTs (sudden confusion).
item.why: A review says 3 to 5 in 100 of them do, and that about 1 to 4 in 100 hospital patients with the DTs die. Most of these figures are passed on by that review or come from old trials.

item.statement: Drinking coffee raises your risk of lung cancer.
item.why: A link between coffee and lung cancer disappeared in people who had never smoked: people who smoke tend to drink more coffee. These studies only watched people.

item.statement: Headaches from skipping caffeine come from expecting them, not from the missing caffeine.
item.why: Before a small operation, people who drank lots of caffeine got caffeine or identical dummy pills, and neither they nor the doctor checking symptoms knew which. By evening, 10 of 20 on dummy pills had a headache and none on caffeine did, though only 40 patients took part and surgery can also cause headaches.

item.statement: Babies whose mothers used cannabis in pregnancy went to newborn intensive care more often.
item.why: Across 19 studies, mostly from before 2000, these babies were also about 109 grams lighter. But many mothers also smoked or drank, and most studies couldn't tell that apart from cannabis.

item.statement: In a lab test, a beta-blocker given after cocaine made heart blood flow drop further.
item.why: Cocaine narrowed their heart arteries a little, and after propranolol, blood flow fell further in all 10 heart patients, none of whom had used cocaine before. What that means for heart attacks is unknown.

item.statement: Most people in treatment for cocaine say they've had paranoia or similar symptoms with it.
item.why: In a review of 17 studies, 68 in 100 said so, while strict diagnostic interviews found a psychotic disorder in 16 in 100. Many also used alcohol or other drugs, so the review can't show cocaine alone caused it.

item.statement: Official records name the drug involved in nearly every overdose death.
item.why: In US records from 1999 to 2015, about 23 in 100 overdose deaths had only an 'unspecified drug' code. The gaps differ by place and rules, and most evidence concerns older US opioid deaths.

item.statement: People who've quit ketamine do worse on memory tests than people who don't use it.
item.why: In one London team's study, 30 people who had stopped for at least a month did as well as people who don't use ketamine, and still did a year later. But most had used less than people who used most days, so this doesn't show stopping fixed anything.

item.statement: Kratom shows up in a large share of US overdose deaths.
item.why: In 27 US states in 2016–17, kratom was found in 152 of 27,338 overdose deaths, about 6 in 1,000. Testing for kratom varied and wasn't recorded, so some deaths with it were probably missed.

item.statement: In one study, more babies exposed to ecstasy in pregnancy had birth defects than expected.
item.why: 12 of 78 babies born alive, about 15 in 100, had a birth defect, against the 2 to 3 in 100 the authors expected. But there was no comparison group, almost half the enquiries were lost to follow-up, and many pregnancies also involved other drugs.

item.statement: In one study, violent crime was the crime most tied to months of meth use.
item.why: Among 469 people dependent on meth in Australia, the link was strongest for selling drugs and property crime, even after money and housing problems were counted. People reported use and crime for the same months, so it can't show which came first.

item.statement: In the largest trial, drug tests confirmed the antidepressant mirtazapine cut meth use.
item.why: People on mirtazapine said they used meth about 2 fewer days in 4 weeks than people on a dummy pill, but saliva drug tests showed no difference, and most kept using. Two small San Francisco trials did find fewer meth-positive urine tests.

item.statement: Most people who use meth end up diagnosed with psychosis.
item.why: In Taiwan, an estimated 4 in 100 adults arrested for using amphetamine-type drugs got a psychosis diagnosis within 10 years, against under 1 in 100 with no drug record. No study has settled which comes first.

item.statement: US deaths involving meth were still rising in 2023.
item.why: They went from about 550 in 1999 to about 35,000 in 2023, though the rise slowed after 2021. Many of these deaths also involved fentanyl or other opioids.

item.statement: The grumpiness and restlessness of quitting smoking usually last for months.
item.why: Most of these feelings were strongest in the first week and gone within 2 to 4 weeks, though for some people they lasted longer or came back. That comes from one expert's summary of older studies.

item.statement: A bad reaction to PCP always wears off within about a day.
item.why: In three cases reported in 1975, a severe breakdown after drugs thought to contain PCP lasted two to four weeks, then passed. Only three cases, and nobody tested the drugs they'd taken.

item.statement: Two months on, most volunteers in one lab study ranked their psilocybin session among their five most meaningful experiences.
item.why: About 2 in 3 put it in their top five, and most who answered said it had raised their wellbeing. But everyone in the study already took part in religious or spiritual activities, which may have shaped how they saw it.

item.statement: The risk of dying is highest in the first week after leaving prison.
item.why: In death records of about 1.5 million people, days 2 to 7 after release carried about 1.5 to 2 times the risk of later weeks, and drug or alcohol poisoning was the top recorded cause. Tolerance was never measured, so the records can't say why.

item.statement: Few people who go to harm reduction sites use drugs alone.
item.why: In a survey at 27 sites in British Columbia, about 3 in 4 had used alone at least once in the past week, most often because it was easier and more comfortable at home. It's one survey, of people already going to these sites.

item.statement: In one big survey, people sought emergency treatment more often after LSD than after magic mushrooms.
item.why: About 10 in 1,000 people who'd used LSD in the past year said they had, mostly for panic, anxiety or confusion, against 2 in 1,000 after magic mushrooms. Nobody checked the answers, or whether the drug was really LSD.

item.statement: Teen cannabis use went up after US states made recreational cannabis legal.
item.why: Not in one big study of 1.4 million US high school answers: after recreational laws, teens were a bit less likely to say they'd used it in the past month. But only 7 states had surveys from before and after, and only for the first few years.

item.statement: Eating poppy seeds can make you fail a sports drug test.
item.why: In a German study, all 9 people who ate poppy seed cake went over the sports limit of the time for morphine in their urine. But the cake used the strongest of 8 seed products tested, and workplace tests weren't studied.

item.statement: A negative xylazine test strip means there's no xylazine.
item.why: With less xylazine than strips are made to find, only 6 of 28 samples read positive, against 37 of 38 with at least that much. That was one batch of strips, read in a lab, on residues from used equipment.

item.statement: In a big trial for hard-to-treat depression, psilocybin's benefit was still clear at 12 weeks.
item.why: In 233 adults across 10 countries, only the full dose beat a tiny one at 3 weeks, and by 12 weeks the gap could be chance.

item.statement: In a trial of psilocybin against an antidepressant, people expected nearly twice as much from psilocybin.
item.why: Allowing for those higher hopes, the team found no clear gap between psilocybin and escitalopram on any of six scales. With 59 people, the trial was too small to show the two work equally well.

item.statement: In a UK study, readers judged a man who died from drugs more harshly than a woman.
item.why: With story details picked at random, readers were also harsher when the story said heroin rather than ecstasy, or an older person with years of use. The differences were small to moderate, and readers answered straight after one made-up story.

item.statement: Most US soldiers who were hooked on narcotics in Vietnam stayed hooked after coming home.
item.why: About 20 in 100 said they'd been dependent on narcotics in Vietnam, but only about 1 in 100 since coming home. How many got treatment wasn't reported.

item.statement: MDMA only raises body temperature when people dance in hot, crowded places.
item.why: Even resting in a room at about 23 degrees, 24 in 100 lab volunteers went over 38 degrees after MDMA, against 9 in 100 after a dummy pill. Heat, dancing and crowds weren't tested.

item.statement: Cannabis medicines have hardly any side effects.
item.why: In trials, about 81 in 100 people on cannabis medicines had at least one, such as dizziness or dry mouth, against 62 in 100 on a dummy or another medicine, and more quit because of them. The trials were short, and long-term harms weren't studied.

item.statement: CBD products usually contain what their labels say.
item.why: In a 2016 US test of 84 CBD products sold online, only about 3 in 10 matched their CBD label, and about 1 in 5 also held THC. Shop products, or today's, may differ.

item.statement: People who had their first drink at 14 or younger more often had alcohol dependence than late starters.
item.why: In a big US survey, about 4 to 5 in 10 who started at 14 or younger had been dependent at some time, against 8 in 100 who started at 25 or older. But people had to remember their first drink, and some of the link seems to come from things that lead to both.

item.statement: People who started using drugs at 13 or younger more often became dependent than later starters.
item.why: In a US survey of adults who'd used drugs at least 12 times, about 1 in 3 who started by 13 had been dependent, against about 1 in 7 who started at 21 or older. A big twin study found much of the link runs in families, so starting young isn't shown to be the cause.

item.statement: Ecstasy pills always contain MDMA.
item.why: A 2004 review of pill tests estimated that only 50 to 80 in 100 held MDMA in the mid-1990s, though nearly all did by the early 2000s; others held related drugs, things like ketamine or caffeine, or nothing active. The tests end around 2002, so pills today may differ.

item.statement: Ecstasy has been shown to damage dopamine nerve cells in people.
item.why: The study that claimed this harm was withdrawn because its animals got a different drug, and five human scan studies showed no clear dopamine change. But very little has been measured in people, so this doesn't show it's safe.

item.statement: The serotonin changes seen on scans of people who used ecstasy are known to be permanent.
item.why: Nobody knows: three studies found more of the scan marker in people who had stopped longer ago, two found no link with time, and no one has been scanned while using and again years later.

item.statement: In a global study, alcohol was the top risk factor for death among people aged 15 to 49.
item.why: The Global Burden of Disease study put about 12 in 100 deaths of men and 4 in 100 of women at those ages down to alcohol. These are computer estimates, not counted deaths.

item.statement: Most people who keep using ecstasy say it stops working as well.
item.why: In questionnaires retold in one review, most said the first time was the strongest. But nobody checked what the tablets held, different people were compared rather than followed, and no lab study has tested it.

item.statement: Clonidine and lofexidine barely help with heroin withdrawal.
item.why: In three trials, about 19 in 100 on them had bad withdrawal, against about 59 in 100 on a dummy pill, and more finished treatment. But the trials were small and old, and none included people coming off fentanyl.

item.statement: An SSRI antidepressant that dulls MDMA's effects also lowers MDMA levels in your blood.
item.why: In 12 men, the SSRI paroxetine lessened MDMA's rises in blood pressure, heart rate and pupil size, yet the MDMA peak in their blood was about 1 in 6 higher. Only healthy volunteers were tested, for a few days at most.

item.statement: When MDMA is found in the blood of someone who died, it usually caused the death.
item.why: In 106 Australian coroners' cases with MDMA in the blood, 6 in 10 died of injuries, such as a crash. A blood test after death can't show who took what, when or why.

item.statement: Reviews rank MDMA with an MAOI antidepressant, like moclobemide, as the riskiest mix they list.
item.why: Four young people in Finland died with MDMA and moclobemide in their blood, and pathologists called each death an accidental poisoning with the two drugs. Four deaths can't give a rate, and all four also had other drugs.

item.statement: Cocaine with alcohol makes the heart beat faster than cocaine alone.
item.why: In 8 people on a hospital ward, heart rate averaged about 84 beats a minute with both, against 74 with cocaine alone. These small studies didn't measure heart attacks or rhythm problems.

item.statement: Meth cravings go away as quickly as the other withdrawal symptoms.
item.why: In one small hospital-ward study, most symptoms eased within one to two weeks and low mood lasted about three, but craving lasted to week five, though weaker. The people in it weren't seeking treatment.

item.statement: If a colour test shows MDMA, the pill has nothing else in it.
item.why: In one small 2003 lab study, seven MDMA samples that also held another drug, like caffeine or amphetamine, gave the same colour as MDMA alone. A review adds that drugs close to MDMA, like MDA, give a similar colour.

item.statement: People who've used both say synthetic cannabis is as enjoyable as ordinary cannabis.
item.why: In a 2011 online survey of about a thousand people who'd used both, they reported much less enjoyment, more bad feelings and more fear of others, and most preferred ordinary cannabis. Nobody tested the products.

item.statement: In lab studies, meth made attention and memory clearly worse at the time.
item.why: In small lab studies, attention, memory and reaction time didn't get measurably worse. But small or moderate harm can't be ruled out, and binges weren't tested.

item.statement: People describe the crash after a cocaine binge as very low mood, then long, heavy sleep.
item.why: Thirty people who sought help for heavy cocaine use also described hunger, and some had passing thoughts of suicide that stayed within the crash. It's what people in treatment told their doctors, so it can't show how often this happens.

item.statement: In UK methadone or buprenorphine treatment, people also prescribed benzos died of poisoning more often.
item.why: Poisoning deaths were about 1 in 100 people a year with a benzo prescription, against 1 in 200 without, even though those on benzos stayed in treatment longer. The study didn't allow for mental health, alcohol or street drug use.

item.statement: Most people on acamprosate in trials still drank again during treatment.
item.why: About 76 in 100 on acamprosate drank again, against 83 in 100 on dummy pills, and the most carefully run trials found no clear difference. Most trials were run or supported by drug companies, mostly its maker.

item.statement: Fewer people went back to heavy drinking on naltrexone than on dummy pills.
item.why: About 46 in 100 on naltrexone went back to heavy drinking, against 54 in 100 on dummy pills; feeling sick, dizziness and vomiting were more common. Most were middle-aged men who had already stopped drinking and had counselling.

item.statement: In old trials, benzodiazepines made seizures during alcohol withdrawal much rarer.
item.why: About 1 in 100 people on a benzodiazepine had a seizure, against about 8 in 100 on dummy pills, and delirium was less common too. The trials ran from the 1960s to 1983, and few people had seizures.

item.statement: Caffeine can set off panic attacks in people with panic disorder.
item.why: In 10 small lab studies, 121 of 237 people with panic disorder had a panic attack after caffeine, and none were reported after a dummy. What ordinary, smaller servings do isn't known.

item.statement: In trials, a CBD medicine at least halved seizures for most children with Dravet syndrome, a severe childhood epilepsy.
item.why: It did for 43 to 49 in 100 children, against 26 to 27 in 100 on a dummy liquid. The maker ran both trials, and in its own backup checks the result didn't always hold up.

item.statement: In sleep labs, people who stopped heavy cannabis use got more dream sleep in the first nights.
item.why: They also slept less and took longer to fall asleep in the first week after stopping. That's from three small studies, two of them from the 1970s, so how long it lasts isn't known.

item.statement: After cocaine, a beta-blocker improves blood flow to the heart.
item.why: In a lab test of 10 heart patients given cocaine, blood flow in the heart fell further in all 10 after the beta-blocker propranolol. None had used cocaine before, and what this means for heart attacks is unknown.

item.statement: Fentanyl test strips can miss some drugs related to fentanyl, like carfentanil.
item.why: In lab tests of 28 related drugs on four brands, three never showed up on any brand, and carfentanil showed only at high amounts. These were mostly pure drugs in water, tested by lab staff.

item.statement: When nobody suspects drugs, a death almost never turns out to be a drug death.
item.why: At one US autopsy centre, drug tests showed that about 49 in 100 of 237 deaths nobody thought were from drugs actually were. Only two US places have been studied, so others may differ.

item.statement: In one twin study, the twin who started cannabis before 17 more often used cocaine or other stimulants.
item.why: It was 48 in 100 against 26 in 100, in Australian twins who grew up together. That's a link, not proof cannabis led on: shared risks and access to other drugs could still explain it.

item.statement: Ketamine's two mirror-image forms, S and R, have the same effects.
item.why: In one study of ten healthy people, the S form raised scores for hallucinations and a changed sense of self in all ten, while the R form brought relaxation. Everyone could tell when they'd been given a drug.

item.statement: In a big trial, ketamine treatment for depression caused more moderate or severe side effects than ECT.
item.why: Within 3 weeks, 25 in 100 on ketamine had a moderate or severe side effect, against 32 in 100 on ECT. Across studies, headache and dizziness were most common, and most side effects soon passed.

item.statement: In a lab study, people's thinking was clearly worse the day after LSD.
item.why: In 24 people, a few memory and word tests went a little better the next morning and one rule-switching puzzle a little worse, which may just be chance. The report gave no mood or sleep data.

item.statement: In small MDMA trials, tiredness was common in the week after a session.
item.why: Five small trials gave MDMA to 58 people with conditions like anxiety or depression; a tight jaw, thirst and sweating were common during sessions, and none of the side effects were serious. The trials were too small to show rare or later harms.

item.statement: People who use meth report much more low mood than people who use other drugs.
item.why: Against people who use other drugs, there was no clear difference. Against people who don't use meth, low mood was somewhat more common, and things like a hard life may explain part of that.

item.statement: People with regular or problematic meth or amphetamine use died nearly 7 times as often as others their age.
item.why: That's about 1 in 90 a year, in studies of people in treatment, in hospital or justice records, or who inject, not everyone who uses. Many also used opioids, so not all of it is the drug.

item.statement: Psychosis linked to meth always clears up within a month of stopping.
item.why: In a typical study, about 1 in 4 people with meth psychosis still had symptoms over a month after stopping. Studies ranged from none to almost all, and most were of hospital patients.

item.statement: In one study, people dependent on meth reported more violent crime in months they used it.
item.why: It was about 12 in 100 months with meth use, against 3 in 100 without, comparing each person with themselves. But use and crime were reported for the same months, so which came first is unclear.

item.statement: Children on the ADHD medicine methylphenidate had trouble falling asleep far more often than on a dummy pill.
item.why: Across 35 trials, it was recorded nearly three times as often with the medicine, though who recorded it changed how big the gap looked. A drug company paid for the review.

item.statement: A death record can say morphine even when the person took heroin.
item.why: In the body, heroin quickly turns into morphine, and some death records named morphine or mixed drugs instead. In the places studied, closer reviews linked more deaths to heroin than the records did.

item.statement: Scans of people with vision problems after poppers mostly showed damaged light-sensing cells at the back of the eye.
item.why: People described blurry or dim vision in the middle; of those scanned again, about 6 in 10 showed the damage improving or clearing. These are reports of about 113 people, so they can't prove poppers caused it or show how often it happens.
